content:Speaker user says: How is Outland different from other sci-fi movies of its time in terms of its setting and portrayal of the future?
Generate according to: Outland was one of the first AA rated movies I ever saw (which is now an obsolete rating in the UK). I remember that I was expecting the worst because the trailer implied that there was at least one exploding head featured during the film. Turns out there were two. Anyway the movie made a strong impression upon me at the age thirteen and I have revisited it numerous times since its release. I recently discovered that Outland had been given a Blu-ray release from Warner Brothers and decided to watch it once again but this time with a more critical eye rather than a nostalgic one.
The story is very straight forward being essentially a western in outer space. Federal Marshal O’Neil is beginning a year’s tour of duty at a major mining facility on Io, one of Jupiter’s moons. After a spate of suicides and random violent crimes, the Marshal discovers that General Manager Sheppard (Peter Boyle) is distributing drugs among the work force to increase productivity. The side effect of long term addiction leads to psychosis. Unable to trust his fellow officers the Marshal find his only ally is the facilities cynical chief medical officer, Dr. Lazarus (Frances Sternhagen). O’Neil’s investigations inevitably lead to him to a show down with two contract killers.
You would have to be an extremely causal viewer not to see shades of High Noon in this movie. But unlike the westerns of the 50’s with their sanitised depiction of the West, this frontier in space is grimy, seedy and altogether plausible. Writer/Director Peter Hyams creates a credible working environment, similar to that of an oilrig. Everything is functional and basic. There is no privacy or glamour. The future is run by big corporations and driven by return on investment. It’s a bleak and rather all too familiar world.
What elevates Outland above the standard of similar genre products from the time is the universally high standard in every aspect of the production. The script is tight, honest and plays to the strengths of the lead actors. The dynamic between Connery and Sternhagen is very plausible, with dry quips, cynicism and grudging respect. The sets are claustrophobic and depressingly credible. The technology on display hasn’t dated too much. Hyams did not make the usual genre mistakes such as exotic costumes and weaponry. The miniature work by Martin J. Bower is outstanding and the Introvision front projection effects works still look acceptable.
Peter Hyams has always been somewhat underrated as a director. All the hallmarks of his previous works are present in Outland. There is a well-crafted chase scene, the mythical “good cop” and corporate/political conspiracies. Of course the movie is not without fault. You can easily question some of the science and there are a few plot wholes. However, the sheer presence of Sean Connery overshadows these minor quibbles. The movie is a showcase for his acting talent which is often overlooked. Outland also demonstrates that can get a lot of mileage from a classic tale and if you are sufficiently inventive. By not involving aliens in this vision of the future and showing that man’s worst enemy in space is himself, the tale maintains credibility.
Outland still remains a finely crafted, character driven thriller. It transcends the usual limitations that some studios impose upon the genre to be a superior piece of film making. There’s not a slack moment in the narrative which is perfectly paced. It would also be remiss of me not to mention the atmospheric score by Jerry Goldsmith. Warner Brothers Blu-ray transfer is very good and the movie looks crisp and clear. Obsessive movie fans you can finally do a comprehensive frame by frame analysis of P.H. Moriarty’s head explosion. For a movie that is thirty one years old, it holds up very well and is still solid entertainment. context:sci-fi keywords: Outland, sci-fi, future, setting, portrayal, Connery, Sternhagen, Peter Hyams, Blu-ray, Sean Connery, Western, corporate, space, movie tags: Sci-fi, dystopian, future, space, movie

content:Speaker user says: Here is a piece of text: The deal to bring the Raiders back to Oakland advanced into the political arena yesterday as the governing boards of Alameda County and Oakland kicked off what is expected to be a smooth, two-week series of approval meetings.
First to huddle yesterday was the county Board of Supervisors, which, after praising a preliminary report, decided unanimously to set a public hearing and final vote on the deal for July 11.
Last night, the Oakland City Council unanimously recommended the deal and set the first of two hearings for 2 p.m. July 5. The second hearing and a final vote by the council are planned for July 11.
Everything from the unabashed enthusiasm of negotiators and elected officials to the near total absence of critics in the crowd pointed to a quick, quiet review process -- in stark contrast to 1990, when two deals to bring back the football team went down in flames after the city and county approved them.
The initial 1990 plan included a $602 million package of stadium improvements, relocation fees and revenue guarantees, putting taxpayers on the hook if sales fell short. The ensuing public outrage sparked a referendum campaign and hundreds of protests at city and county meetings. A quickly crafted replacement deal removing public guarantees fell apart because of engineering concerns, and the fallout from the year's mess left Raiders supporters battered politically.
Five years later, it appears to be an entirely different ballgame.
The 1995 deal to return the Raiders to their hometown 13 years after they defected to Los Angeles will involve no real risk of public money and bring nothing but prestige and cash to Oakland, negotiators told elected officials yesterday.
The surest guarantee of steady income, they said, will be the area's legendary fan support -- and with 63,800 inquiries already logged to Coliseum ticket reservation lines by yesterday afternoon, the assumption seemed to be holding despite average ticket costs of $50 a game.
"There is a sense of new enthusiasm and excitement in the community and a new feeling of pride, and let me tell you, we need that," Oakland Coliseum Board President George Vukasin told the Board of Supervisors. "This deal is sound, it is responsible, it will work."
All indications are that he was preaching to the converted.
County and city officials have not seen the official 16-year lease that would place the Raiders in the Coliseum beginning this season, but condensed details presented to them yesterday brought no surprises. Final language on the agreement is being worked out, and copies should be available before the public hearings, Vukasin said.
Yesterday's report estimates that if the Raiders come to town, annual sales, business and hotel tax revenues will bring $1 million to Oakland and $200,000 to Alameda County. The team also would create about 1,000 full- and part- time jobs, and a $1-per-seat surcharge would raise up to $600,000 a year for Oakland schools and county social programs.
In return, the county and city would issue bonds to pay for $90 million in renovations to the Coliseum -- adding 15,000 seats and 120 luxury boxes -- and to loan the Raiders $31.9 million for relocation and $10 million for a new training facility. Combined with other costs and potential cost overruns, the entire bond package to finance the Raiders deal could reach $150 million to $210 million, most of which would be repaid through ticket sales.
In a worst-case scenario, such as if Raiders games sold poorly for many years running, the city and county might have to pay back the bonds themselves. But negotiators yesterday pooh-poohed such a possibility.
"We feel very strongly that there will be no call on general funds from either the city or the county to repay the bonds," said former county Administrator Steve Szalay, who has been the county's lead negotiator with the Raiders.
Oakland Deputy City Manager Ezra Rapport strongly recommended the deal to the council, saying, "We think it's not a risky transaction because of the strengths of the marketing plan. . . . Even in poor years, there would be no call on city and county general funds."
The only dissent at yesterday's meetings came from David Simon, a certified public accountant from Oakland, who told the county supervisors: "I am viciously against the deal" because it allows the Raiders to "mooch off the county of Alameda." Simon later made similar remarks to the Oakland City Council.
Two potential land mines to the agreement lie with the National Football League, which must approve the Raiders relocation, and the Oakland A's baseball team, who are said to be unhappy with some elements of the deal even though it expands the Coliseum, where they play.
Under the renovations, the number of baseball seats will increase from 44,000 to about 48,000. There would be 65,500 football seats, up from the current 54,000. A's spokeswoman Christina Centeno said yesterday that team management had no comment but was keeping involved in the Raiders plans.
NFL team owners are scheduled to meet in Chicago early next month to vote on the Raiders move. The league lost a costly fight to keep the team in Oakland in the early 1980s, and there appears to be little sentiment for another legal battle.
There was still no word yesterday from Raiders Managing General Partner Al Davis, who last week signed a letter of intent with Vukasin to bring the team north. But Raiders and Coliseum officials said he intends to visit Oakland, probably on July 6, to hail the new agreement.
Davis had planned originally to be in Oakland tomorrow, but the Golden State Warriors -- who play in the Coliseum's arena -- will be conducting their annual players' draft this week, "and Al doesn't want to interfere with their week," said Vukasin.

A play that lives in infamy, at least for Oakland Raiders fans. On a snowy night for the 2001 AFC Divisional playoffs, the Patriots were down 13-10 at home to Oakland, with under two minutes to play. On a first-down play from the Raiders’ 42, Tom Brady’s former Michigan teammate, Charles Woodson, strip-sacked him, untouched on a corner blitz. Brady lost the ball, the Raiders’ Greg Biekert fell on it and it looked like the Patriots were done. But referee Walt Coleman’s crew determined that Brady was in the process of passing the ball when he lost it, invoking the little-used tuck rule. The play went down as an incomplete pass, Brady completed a 13-yard pass to David Patten to get New England in field-goal range, and Adam Vinatieri made a 45-yard field goal despite the wintry conditions to tie the game. Vinatieri hit a 23-yard kick in overtime for the win. Coleman hasn’t officiated a Raiders game since, and the NFL voted to repeal the tuck rule in 2013.
Robert Kraft grew up in Brookline, Massachusetts, and as he says often, spent many Sunday afternoons freezing with his sons on the metal bleachers at the New England Patriots old home stadium as a season ticket holder. Through a series of savvy business moves, Kraft first bought the harness racing track next to the stadium, then more land around the stadium, and then the stadium itself. In 1994, then-Patriots owner James Orthwein offered Kraft $75 million to buy out the remainder of the team’s lease at the stadium, because Orthwein wanted to move the team to St. Louis. Kraft turned Orthwein down and instead offered a then-NFL record $175 million to buy the team outright; the sale was finalized on Jan. 21, 1994. While he toyed with the idea of moving the Patriots to Hartford, Connecticut, Kraft kept them in Foxboro, built a new stadium largely with his own money, and under his stewardship, New England has made the playoffs 18 times in 24 years, making seven Super Bowl appearances and winning five.
28-3. Or, as it read on the Fox graphic, 3-28. With 8:31 left in the third quarter of Super Bowl LI, the Atlanta Falcons seemed headed for their first-ever championship. New England began to come back, which wasn’t too surprising, but 25 points was an almost impossible hole to dig out of. A touchdown late in the third, a field goal early in the fourth, but the Patriots were still down, 28-12 with 9:44 to play. The game turned on third-and-1 from the Atlanta 36 when New England’s Dont’a Hightower strip-sacked Matt Ryan, the Patriots recovered, and Tom Brady got the ball at the Atlanta 25. Five plays later, they had another touchdown, and after a successful two-point conversion, they were within eight points. New England won in overtime, completing the most incredible comeback in Super Bowl history.
The Patriots have had a lot of great on-field moments over the last 15 or so years, but their win over the St. Louis Rams – the Greatest Show on Turf – in Super Bowl XXXVI started a dynasty, in a league that’s not supposed to have dynasties. New England, with Tom Brady starting just his 17th game, in his second season, was a historic underdog (14 points) in the eyes of Las Vegas. But the Patriots’ defense had one mandate above all that night: hit Rams star back Marshall Faulk on every single snap, and the offense just needed to play as mistake-free as possible. When St. Louis tied the game at 17-17 with just 90 seconds to play, New England had no timeouts, and broadcaster John Madden said it should play for overtime. Brady, however, had other ideas. He completed 5-of-8 passes, including a 23-yarder to Troy Brown, and when he walked off the field with just seconds left on the clock, it was for Adam Vinatieri to line up for a 48-yard field goal. Vinatieri made it, and New Englanders, who had supported a largely hapless franchise for years, got to celebrate at last.
It is comical now. The greatest quarterback the league has ever seen, the man for whom no moment has ever seemed too big, could only watch as 198 players, six of them quarterbacks, were taken before him in the 2000 NFL draft. He was skinny, he was slow, he’d had to fight for his job as a senior at Michigan after a highly recruited freshman (Drew Henson) hit campus. Not long after the Patriots took him 199th, Brady passed Kraft in one of the hallways in the team facility.
The kid never lacked in confidence. And he was right. He grew up in Brookline, Massachusetts, and as he says often, spent many Sunday afternoons freezing with his sons on the metal bleachers at the Patriots old home stadium as a season ticket holder.

Through a series of savvy business moves, Kraft first bought the harness racing track next to the stadium, then more land around the stadium, and then the stadium itself. In 1994, then-Patriots owner James Orthwein offered Kraft $75 million to buy out the remainder of the team’s lease at the stadium, because Orthwein wanted to move the team to St. Louis.

Kraft turned Orthwein down and instead offered a then-NFL record $175 million to buy the team outright; the sale was finalized on Jan. 21, 1994. While he toyed with the idea of moving the Patriots to Hartford, Connecticut, Kraft kept them in Foxboro, built a new stadium largely with his own money, and under his stewardship, New England has made the playoffs 18 times in 24 years, making seven Super Bowl appearances and winning five. context:Robert Kraft purchased the New England Patriots, beginning with a harness racing track and expanding to the stadium itself, resulting in playoff success and Super Bowl championships. keywords: Patriots, Robert Kraft, Stadium, Business, Football tags: Business, Sports, Football, Ownership
